performers: London Symphony Orchestra; Pierre Monteux, conductor
intro: Pierre Monteux conducts the London Symphony Orchestra in the complete Symphony No. 2 in D major, Op. 43. A figure of three rising notes in the strings becomes the finale’s main D major theme, and a long crescendo leads from the scherzo into the finale without a break.

sections.label: A · I. Rising three-note string figure
sections.mNote: Short string phrases, each followed by woodwinds and horns.

sections.label: B · Woodwind phrase after a pause
sections.mNote: A longer woodwind phrase breaks into the opening dance.

sections.label: Dev · Pizzicato strings, short phrases
sections.mNote: The strings play pizzicato at the start of the development.

sections.label: Dev · Woodwind phrases, crescendo
sections.mNote: Woodwind phrases take up the opening ideas in a crescendo.

sections.label: A′ · Opening themes in counterpoint
sections.mNote: The opening themes return together in counterpoint.

sections.label: Coda · Opening material returns
sections.mNote: The first movement ends with string phrases from its opening.

sections.label: C · II. Pizzicato basses, bassoon melody
sections.mNote: Cellos and basses play pizzicato beneath the bassoon melody.

sections.label: C′ · Bassoon theme, varied, louder
sections.mNote: The opening theme expands towards the brass climax.

sections.label: D · Contrasting theme in divided strings
C″ · March theme returns
sections.mNote: The bassoon theme returns as a heavy processional.

sections.label: D′ · String theme returns, rising
sections.mNote: The string theme returns and expands between interruptions.

sections.label: E · Melody in fragments after the climax
sections.mNote: The bass breaks off the long melody; only fragments follow.

sections.label: Coda · Another climb, two plucked notes
sections.mNote: The slow movement gathers again and ends with pizzicato.

sections.label: F · III. Vivacissimo, fast strings
sections.mNote: Fast string figures under longer wind phrases.

sections.label: G · Trio, oboe in G♭ major
sections.mNote: The slow trio opens with nine repeated notes on the oboe.

sections.label: F′ · Scherzo returns, strings and horns
sections.mNote: The scherzo returns, with a new rising figure in the horns.

sections.label: G′ · Trio returns, oboe melody
sections.mNote: The slow oboe melody returns before the bridge to the finale.

sections.label: Link · Three rising notes
sections.mNote: G♭–A♭–B♭ forms the bridge between movements.

sections.label: H · IV. D major theme, strings and trumpets
sections.mNote: The broad D major theme is built on three rising notes.

sections.label: I · Contrasting theme over march accompaniment
sections.mNote: The contrasting theme is set over a marching accompaniment.

sections.label: J · Oboe phrases after the march
sections.mNote: Oboe phrases follow the march.

sections.label: H′ · String theme returns, fuller scoring
sections.mNote: The broad tune returns with sharper woodwind figures around it.

sections.label: I′ · Contrasting march theme returns
sections.mNote: The contrasting theme returns before the final build.

sections.label: Coda · Rising four-note figure, D major
sections.mNote: The rising figure extends to a fourth note.

cues.title: Opening three-note figure, strings
cues.text: The strings begin with three rising notes in D major. Woodwinds and horns follow in short phrases separated by rests. The three-note figure returns in the finale.
cues.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, account of Symphony No. 2, first-movement discussion and score extract 7; the finale discussion identifies the returning three-note figure. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Rapallo sketches, February 1901
cues.text: In February 1901 Sibelius was in Rapallo, Italy, sketching a theme for the slow movement. On the back of the sheet he wrote a scene for Don Juan, in which a guest entered his castle and stayed silent. When the guest started to sing, Don Juan recognised Death.
cues.evidence: Ilkka Oramo, Los Angeles Philharmonic programme note on Symphony No. 2: the Don Juan vision (“a guest enters … He remains mute. Eventually he starts singing”) written on a sheet whose reverse Sibelius dated 2/19/01 and used to sketch the D-minor bassoon theme of the slow movement. The Sibelius Society of Finland dates the Rapallo sketches to February 1901. https://www.laphil.com/musicdb/pieces/3934/symphony-no-2 https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm

cues.title: Letter from Axel Carpelan, 1900
cues.text: In 1900 Axel Carpelan, the baron who gave Finlandia its name, wrote to Sibelius that “it is high time for you to travel”. Italy, he added, taught “cantabile, balance and harmony”. Carpelan had no money himself, so he found a patron to pay for the trip.
cues.evidence: Axel Carpelan to Sibelius, 1900 (“You have been sitting at home for quite a while, Mr. Sibelius, it is high time for you to travel”), quoted by Ilkka Oramo in the Los Angeles Philharmonic programme note: the Italian winter, the penniless baron’s patron, the family’s departure in October 1900 and arrival in Italy at the end of January 1901. https://www.laphil.com/musicdb/pieces/3934/symphony-no-2

cues.title: Wasenius’s recollection of the first sketches
cues.text: The publisher Karl Fredrik Wasenius recalled Sibelius staring at a little piece by a seven-year-old girl, then starting to improvise: “Now I’ve got the thing that I’ve been waiting for weeks! Now it came!” Wasenius said these were motifs for the first movement of this symphony.
cues.evidence: Wasenius’s recollection, reported by the Sibelius Society of Finland: https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm

cues.title: Form of the first movement
cues.text: Scholars have found it hard to identify a clear second subject in this movement. It opens with a series of aphoristic fragments, and their connections become clear only gradually. Veijo Murtomäki described the unity as “something discovered by Sibelius during the process of composition”.
cues.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, first-movement discussion, quoting Veijo Murtomäki: https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm

cues.title: Recapitulation, first movement
cues.text: In the recapitulation the opening dance and the longer woodwind theme return together. Sibelius sets them against each other in counterpoint, with one phrase moving while the other plays a sustained line across it.
cues.evidence: Paul Serotsky’s score-based programme note describes the first movement’s recapitulation with both main subjects together in counterpoint. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/sibelius_sym2.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Reception in Finland, 1902
cues.text: Finland was then subject to the tsar’s russification programme. After the première in March 1902 the public heard the heroic first and last movements as exactly what it needed, and the symphony was quickly taken up as an emblem of national liberation. Sibelius denied any such programme.
cues.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland: the heroic and optimistic first and final movements were exactly what the Finnish public needed in 1902, during a period of Russian oppression. Ilkka Oramo, Los Angeles Philharmonic programme note: immediately after the première of 8 March 1902 the symphony was appropriated as an emblem of national liberation, in the Grand Duchy’s russification years of 1899–1905, and Sibelius categorically denied programmatic readings. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm https://www.laphil.com/musicdb/pieces/3934/symphony-no-2

cues.title: Second movement opening, D minor
cues.text: The slow movement opens in D minor. Cellos and double basses play a long pizzicato line before the bassoons enter with the theme.
cues.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, second-movement discussion and score extract 8: pizzicato cellos and double basses, then bassoon theme. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm . D minor: IMSLP work catalogue, https://imslp.org/wiki/Symphony_No.2,_Op.43_(Sibelius,_Jean).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Monteux and Brahms, Vienna
cues.text: As a young man in Vienna with the Geloso Quartet, Monteux took part in a private performance of a Brahms quartet with the composer listening. Brahms told the players: “It takes the French to play my music properly. The Germans all play it much too heavily.”
cues.evidence: Decca Classics, Pierre Monteux: The Complete Decca/Philips Recordings, booklet essay (printed p. 48): Monteux in Vienna with the Geloso Quartet and Brahms’s remark. https://d24ku69pnn7av2.cloudfront.net/decca-classics-booklets/2020/02894834711X_Pierre_Monteux_Booklet.pdf

cues.title: Return of the bassoon theme
cues.text: The bassoon theme returns, fiercer, as the anxiety grows. Sibelius printed no programme, but his sketches name Don Juan and Death, and the music can be heard as an argument between them, with Don Juan’s desperate pleas and Death’s inevitable answers.
cues.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, second-movement discussion: the bassoon theme, the increasing anxiety, and Don Juan’s desperate arguments and death’s inevitable answers. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second theme, divided strings
cues.text: After the brass climax and a pause, divided strings play a long, quiet melody, the movement’s second theme, in F♯ major. Sibelius headed its early sketch “Christus”. The theme is interrupted several times later in the movement.
cues.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, second-movement discussion and score extract 9, identifies the Christ theme. Ilkka Oramo, Los Angeles Philharmonic programme note: the C-major theme drafted in Florence, two months after Rapallo, under the word “Christus”, which became the movement’s second theme in F♯ major. Divided-string scoring and the preceding brass climax are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._2_(Sibelius). https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm https://www.laphil.com/musicdb/pieces/3934/symphony-no-2
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Monteux and the London Symphony Orchestra
cues.text: Pierre Monteux, born in Paris on 4 April 1875, began working with the London Symphony Orchestra in 1957. In 1961 the self-governing orchestra invited him to become its principal conductor. He was then in his eighties, and the orchestra offered him a 25-year contract with an option for renewal.
cues.evidence: Decca Classics, Pierre Monteux: The Complete Decca/Philips Recordings, booklet essay (printed pp. 48–51): birth date, the 1957 start of the LSO relationship, the 1961 invitation and 25-year contract. https://d24ku69pnn7av2.cloudfront.net/decca-classics-booklets/2020/02894834711X_Pierre_Monteux_Booklet.pdf

cues.title: Robert Kajanus on the Andante, 1902
cues.text: In 1902 the conductor Robert Kajanus heard in the Andante “the most crushing protest against all the injustice” that threatens to take the light from the sun. Sibelius’s own sketches refer to Don Juan and Death.
cues.evidence: Robert Kajanus, 1902, quoted by the Sibelius Society of Finland: https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm . Ilkka Oramo’s Los Angeles Philharmonic note quotes the same passage in another translation (“the most broken-hearted protest against all the injustice”). https://www.laphil.com/musicdb/pieces/3934/symphony-no-2

cues.title: Premières, Helsinki 1902 and Stockholm 1903
cues.text: Sibelius conducted the première in Helsinki on 8 March 1902. He revised the symphony afterwards, and his brother-in-law Armas Järnefelt conducted the new version in Stockholm on 10 November 1903.
cues.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland gives both premières, conductors and versions. Armas Järnefelt is Aino Sibelius’s brother. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm

cues.title: First performance, 8 March 1902
cues.text: Oscar Merikanto reported that the first performance, on 8 March 1902, “exceeded even the highest expectations”. Its success consolidated Sibelius’s fame as a national hero.
cues.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, account of Symphony No. 2, quoting Oscar Merikanto on the première of 8 March 1902: https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm

cues.title: Scherzo, string figures and flute
cues.text: In the scherzo the strings play rapid repeated figures. Slower phrases in the wind sound above them, and the flute’s line moves at a much slower pace than the string figures below.
cues.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, scherzo discussion and score extract 10: fast string figures under the flute theme. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Robert Kajanus on the scherzo, 1902
cues.text: In 1902 the conductor Robert Kajanus described the scherzo as frenetic preparation, writing that “Everyone piles his straw on the haystack” and that every second “seems to last an hour”. For him the oboe trio in G♭ major showed “what is at stake”.
cues.evidence: Robert Kajanus, 1902, on the scherzo, in Ilkka Oramo’s Los Angeles Philharmonic programme note: “Everyone piles his straw on the haystack, all fibers are strained and every second seems to last an hour”; the oboe motive in G-flat major shows “what is at stake”. The Sibelius Society of Finland quotes his “hurried preparation” in another translation. https://www.laphil.com/musicdb/pieces/3934/symphony-no-2 https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm

cues.title: Trio in G♭ major, oboe
cues.text: The trio slows the dance and moves to G♭ major. An oboe repeats the same note nine times over clarinets and horns before its melody opens out.
cues.evidence: Nine repeated notes: Sibelius Society of Finland, score extract 11, https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm . G♭ major and clarinet-and-horn accompaniment: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._2_(Sibelius).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Repeat of the scherzo
cues.text: The scherzo returns with changes. Sibelius alters the slower phrases that guide the fast string writing and adds a new rising figure for the horns.
cues.evidence: Paul Serotsky’s programme note on the repeat of the scherzo: https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/sibelius_sym2.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the trio
cues.text: In 1902 the repeat of the scherzo would have been expected to end the movement. Here the oboe trio returns after it, and this return leads into the bridge to the finale.
cues.evidence: Paul Serotsky’s programme note: the scherzo’s repeat would have been expected to end the movement in 1902, and the return of the trio raised eyebrows. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/sibelius_sym2.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Link from scherzo to finale
cues.text: Joining two movements was an old idea; Paul Serotsky called the way Sibelius did it “utterly new”. The last bars of the scherzo grow louder and lead directly into the finale. The finale’s ground-plan follows the scherzo’s, including its surprise ending.
cues.evidence: Paul Serotsky’s programme note: the link between the third and fourth movements and the finale’s ground-plan following the scherzo’s. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/sibelius_sym2.htm

cues.title: Opening of the finale in D major
cues.text: The scherzo’s long crescendo leads without a break into the finale. The strings play the three-note rising figure in D major, and the trumpets reply, a role the woodwinds took in the first movement.
cues.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, bridge and finale discussion, score extract 12: rising figure, D major strings and trumpet answer. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm . The continuous join is also documented in the recording’s movement list: https://archive.org/details/sibelius-2-compl-monteux-lso .
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Finale oboe motif and Elli Järnefelt
cues.text: Aino Sibelius said that the oboe motif in the finale was written in memory of her sister, Elli Järnefelt, who had taken her own life. The passage brings a sense of the sacred into the music. This recedes when the faster music resumes.
cues.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, final-movement discussion: the oboe motif, Aino Sibelius’s statement about Elli Järnefelt, and the sense of the sacred. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm

cues.title: Kingsway Hall, June 1958
cues.text: Monteux and the London Symphony recorded the symphony at Kingsway Hall on 18–20 June 1958. John Culshaw produced, Kenneth Wilkinson was the balance engineer, and RCA first issued the result in October 1959 as LSC 2342.
cues.evidence: Decca Classics, Pierre Monteux: The Complete Decca/Philips Recordings, booklet PDF page 21 (printed p. 40): recording location and dates, producer, balance engineer, first release. https://d24ku69pnn7av2.cloudfront.net/decca-classics-booklets/2020/02894834711X_Pierre_Monteux_Booklet.pdf

cues.title: Christening in Ruovesi, 1899
cues.text: At the christening of the painter Akseli Gallen-Kallela’s son in Ruovesi, in the summer of 1899, Sibelius improvised a theme that went into the finale of this symphony.
cues.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, account of Symphony No. 2: the improvisation at the christening of Gallen-Kallela’s son in Ruovesi, summer 1899. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm

cues.title: Critical reception, Flodin and Thomson
cues.text: In 1903 the critic Karl Flodin called the symphony “an absolute masterpiece”, pointing the way of Beethoven’s. Virgil Thomson later called it “vulgar, self-indulgent and provincial beyond any description”. It is the most played of Sibelius’s symphonies.
cues.evidence: Karl Flodin (1903) and Virgil Thomson, quoted by the Sibelius Society of Finland, which also calls the Second the most popular and most frequently recorded of the symphonies. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm

cues.title: Coda in D major
cues.text: The rising three-note figure returns in the closing D major music. Late in the coda it is extended to a fourth note, which it has not reached earlier in the symphony. Erkki Salmenhaara identified this extension.
cues.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, final-movement discussion, credits Erkki Salmenhaara with identifying the late extension of the three-note figure. The cue covers the coda as a whole. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Pause before the woodwind second subject
transitions.from: A · I. Rising three-note string figure
transitions.to: B · Woodwind phrase after a pause
transitions.how: The opening dance stops for a pause. The woodwinds then play a longer phrase, the start of the second-subject group, after the strings’ short, separated answers.
transitions.evidence: Paul Serotsky, first-movement discussion: pause, then the woodwind second-subject group. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/sibelius_sym2.htm

transitions.title: Pizzicato strings open the development
transitions.from: B · Woodwind phrase after a pause
transitions.how: The development begins with pizzicato strings. A rocking phrase and short woodwind figures are added above them, and the string rhythm from the opening continues underneath the new phrases.
transitions.evidence: Paul Serotsky, first-movement discussion: pizzicato at the development, rocking phrase, woodwind theme and continuing opening accompaniment. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/sibelius_sym2.htm

transitions.title: The two themes return together
transitions.how: The crescendo relaxes, and the opening dance theme returns alongside the longer woodwind phrase. The two themes, each in its own rhythm, are combined in counterpoint and sound at the same time.
transitions.evidence: Paul Serotsky, first-movement discussion of the recapitulation. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/sibelius_sym2.htm

transitions.title: From D major to plucked D minor
transitions.to: C · II. Pizzicato basses, bassoon melody
transitions.how: The first movement ends in D major. After the break, cellos and basses open the slow movement in D minor and play a long plucked line. The bassoons then join them. The movement is marked Tempo andante, ma rubato, which means a walking pace with free rubato.
transitions.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, first- and second-movement discussions; movement keys and heading in the IMSLP work catalogue. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm ; https://imslp.org/wiki/Symphony_No.2,_Op.43_(Sibelius,_Jean)

transitions.title: Divided strings follow the brass climax
transitions.to: D · Contrasting theme in divided strings
transitions.how: The brass climax stops and a pause follows. Divided strings then begin the contrasting melody softly, in long phrases after the broken calls of the preceding passage. Sibelius headed his sketch for this theme “Christus”.
transitions.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, second-movement discussion and score extract 9; scoring and pause described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._2_(Sibelius). https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm

transitions.title: Bass phrase interrupts the string melody
transitions.to: E · Melody in fragments after the climax
transitions.how: The long string melody of the second theme rises to its climax. A contrary phrase in the bass, a variant of the same theme, then interrupts it. The music breaks into quiet fragments for the coda, and pieces of the earlier tune return.
transitions.evidence: Paul Serotsky, second-movement discussion: the second theme’s climax is interrupted by its bass variant before the fragmentary coda. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/sibelius_sym2.htm

transitions.title: Pizzicato close into the Vivacissimo
transitions.from: Coda · Another climb, two plucked notes
transitions.how: The slow movement ends on two pizzicato strokes. After the break the Vivacissimo begins, with the strings playing fast repeated figures and the woodwind playing longer phrases above them.
transitions.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, slow-movement ending and scherzo discussion, score extract 10. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm

transitions.title: Scherzo to trio: oboe on one note
transitions.to: G · Trio, oboe in G♭ major
transitions.how: The fast string figures stop. The trio moves to G♭ major, and an oboe repeats one note nine times over clarinets and horns. The melody then grows out of that repeated note.
transitions.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, score extract 11; G♭ major and accompaniment described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._2_(Sibelius). https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm

transitions.title: Horns add a rising figure
transitions.from: G · Trio, oboe in G♭ major
transitions.to: F′ · Scherzo returns, strings and horns
transitions.how: The scherzo returns with its fast string figures. Sibelius alters the slower phrases above them and adds a rising figure in the horns, played over the same string accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Paul Serotsky, scherzo discussion: altered slower phrases and new rising horn figure in the return. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/sibelius_sym2.htm

transitions.title: The oboe trio returns
transitions.from: F′ · Scherzo returns, strings and horns
transitions.how: The rapid string figures of the scherzo die away and the slow trio returns. The oboe melody comes back to the foreground. On this second appearance the trio is not followed by the scherzo. It continues into the rising bridge that leads without a break into the finale.
transitions.evidence: Paul Serotsky, scherzo and finale discussion: second trio and continuous transition. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/sibelius_sym2.htm

transitions.title: Rising G♭–A♭–B♭ leads into the finale
transitions.how: The trio turns into a crescendo built on the rising notes G♭–A♭–B♭, which the Sibelius Society of Finland identifies as the bridge motif. The three notes follow the rising shape heard at the start of the symphony. The motif is repeated several times, which lengthens the crescendo. The finale’s main theme then enters in D major.
transitions.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland identifies G♭–A♭–B♭ as the bridge motif and D major as the finale’s arrival. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm

transitions.title: Scherzo into finale without a break
transitions.to: H · IV. D major theme, strings and trumpets
transitions.how: The crescendo leads directly into D major. The strings play the three-note rise as a broad melody, and the trumpets reply. The finale’s Allegro moderato begins straight out of the bridge, with no silence between the movements.
transitions.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, finale discussion and score extract 12; the recording’s movement list also specifies the continuous join. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm ; https://archive.org/details/sibelius-2-compl-monteux-lso

transitions.title: Woodwind figures around the returning tune
transitions.from: J · Oboe phrases after the march
transitions.to: H′ · String theme returns, fuller scoring
transitions.how: A long crescendo begins at the quiet passage and leads to the return of the broad string tune. Short woodwind figures enter around the melody and keep a sharper rhythm against its long phrases.
transitions.evidence: Paul Serotsky, finale discussion: gradual build to the main theme’s reprise with active woodwind figures. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/sibelius_sym2.htm

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: Both the Internet Archive description and the Decca booklet credit the London Symphony Orchestra under Monteux. The leader and principals on this session are not documented here; the booklet’s essay says that Hugh Maguire joined as leader after the orchestra’s 1957 arrival of young players, without tying that to this date.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: The 1903 final version, as published by Fazer & Westerlund (the version in general use); the performing edition of this recording has not been checked against a score
fields.note: The Sibelius Society gives the first version (premiere 8 March 1902) and the final version of 1903. The 1958 recording would normally use the published score; the Decca booklet lists Breitkopf & Härtel as publisher of the edition. No source states which version Monteux used, and no score alignment was made.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The Decca booklet gives Kingsway Hall, 18–20 June 1958, for the disc whose track list holds this symphony (PDF page 21, printed p. 40, beside the track list on PDF page 20, printed p. 39; the 24 and 25 June 1958 sessions marked with an asterisk are for Elgar’s Enigma Variations on the same disc). The Internet Archive description narrows the date to 20 June 1958 without a source. The identification rests on the layout of the booklet’s credits, which the author read as attaching to the disc listing Sibelius and Elgar; the measured movement lengths of this file (10:17, 14:36, 6:14 and 12:49) match the booklet’s track times (10:16, 14:36, 6:15, 12:49).

fields.label: Label
fields.value: RCA (US catalogue LSC 2342; UK catalogue SB 207); Decca reissue SDD 234 (September 1970)
fields.note: The booklet’s “First released as” line names the catalogue numbers and months but not the label name for SB 207. The Internet Archive description says Decca–RCA. The author treats the first issue as RCA’s.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The first issue was in October 1959 (LSC 2342) and May 1960 (SB 207); both dates are before 1963.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: The booklet names no matrix, take or side numbers.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The Internet Archive item was uploaded by a private account (subject tag “DWTKenInNY”); its description names no transfer engineer or source disc.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The item’s public date is 11 June 2023; that is an upload date, not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: A single VBR MP3 of the whole symphony; the uploader’s movement times are given in the description

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Sibelius died in 1957, so the symphony (published 1903) is in copyright in countries with a life-plus-70 term, including the EU, until the end of 2027; IMSLP records it as public domain in the United States, Canada and life-plus-50 countries
fields.note: The IMSLP work page carries a notice that the work is not in the public domain in life-plus-70 countries. The end date of 2027 is computed from Sibelius’s death in 1957, which the site’s Sibelius biography gives as 20 September 1957. This dossier does not claim the composition is out of copyright in the EU. The programme’s rule applies to the sound recording, not the composition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — EU public domain (territorial): first published before 1963 (RCA LSC 2342, October 1959; SB 207, May 1960).
fields.note: Territorial only: the recording’s first publication in 1959–60 predates 1963, so its EU 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. The United States status of a 1958–59 sound recording is not established here. The Internet Archive item carries no licence URL; its metadata and description contain no non-commercial restriction. The item belongs to a general “folksoundomy” collection and was uploaded by a third party, not by the rights holder.

composer.born: 8 December 1865, Hämeenlinna, Grand Duchy of Finland
composer.epithet: Composer who took the horn theme of his Fifth Symphony from sixteen swans he watched circling over Ainola, and who worked on the symphony for four years.
facts: Wegelius in Helsinki, 1885–89; Becker in Berlin; Fuchs and Goldmark in Vienna
Ainola, Lars Sonck’s timber house near Lake Tuusula, from 1904
Swedish at home; Finnish at school and in Kullervo and Luonnotar
Seven symphonies, one violin concerto, tone poems, theatre music, songs and chamber music
composer.background:
In Vienna in 1891, Sibelius auditioned for the Philharmonic and failed. He wanted to be a violinist; the jury found him too nervous even for an orchestral post. He was twenty-five, studying composition with Robert Fuchs and Karl Goldmark, spending money he did not have at parties and going to as much of the city’s music as he could. After hearing Bruckner’s Third Symphony he thought its author the greatest living composer. In his lodgings during the same period he was studying the rhythms of the Finnish Kalevala.

He was born in Hämeenlinna in 1865, when Finland was a grand duchy of the Russian Empire. His father, a doctor, died three years later, leaving debts. At home the family spoke Swedish; at school Janne learnt Finnish. He played chamber music with his sister Linda and brother Christian, and in 1885 went to Helsinki, nominally to study law. He was soon spending his days at Martin Wegelius’s Music Institute, where he befriended Ferruccio Busoni and worked through quartets by Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven. He took his professional name from a dead uncle’s visiting cards, which he had found. “Jean is now my musical name,” he told Uncle Pehr on 31 March 1886. After Helsinki he studied with Albert Becker in Berlin, and then in Vienna.
